name: Carbon Sequestration Practices
region: Global (Amazonia, West Africa, East Asia, Northern Europe, Pacific Islands)
summary: Deliberate and incidental practices that capture atmospheric carbon and lock it into soils, biomass, or durable materials — from ancient biochar production to agroforestry and peat management.

claims.statement: Terra preta soils in Amazonia sequester carbon for millennia via biochar; radiocarbon dating shows stable carbon pools 2000+ years old, proving that human land management can create permanent carbon sinks
Traditional agroforestry systems (forest gardens) in Southeast Asia, West Africa, and Mesoamerica sequester 2–9x more carbon per hectare than monoculture, while maintaining food production
Indigenous fire management (cultural burning) in Australia and North America maintains ecosystem carbon balance and prevents catastrophic wildfire carbon release

evidence.source: Glaser et al. (2001) The 'Terra Preta' Phenomenon: A Model for Sustainable Agriculture in the Humid Tropics, Naturwissenschaften 88(1)
Lehmann et al. (2006) Bio-char Sequestration in Terrestrial Ecosystems — A Review, Mitigation and Adaptation Strategies for Global Change 11(2)
Nair (2012) Carbon Sequestration Studies in Agroforestry Systems: A Reality-Check, Agroforestry Systems 86(2)
Gammage (2011) The Biggest Estate on Earth: How Aborigines Made Australia, Allen & Unwin

notes: Resolves 2 inbound links (terra_preta, regenerative_agriculture). The bridge between ancient soil management and modern climate mitigation. Indigenous practices are the proof-of-concept for what industrial carbon capture is trying to achieve.
